newsitem.title: MONACO: ATHLETICS-BAILEY PLAYS SECOND FIDDLE TO JOHNSON.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BAILEY PLAYS SECOND FIDDLE TO JOHNSON.

text.p: Olympic 100 metres gold medallists and world heavyweight boxing champions have always enjoyed special status in the world of sports.
The first has traditionally been lauded as the world's fastest man; the second is usually dubbed the world's best fighter.

Evander Holyfield's comprehensive demolition of the fearsome Mike Tyson for one of the four versions of the world heavyweight title this year established him in most people's eyes as the world's greatest boxer.

But Canadian Donovan Bailey, world and Olympic champion over 100 metres, has found to his evident frustration that a world record in the Atlanta Olympics 100 metres final last July still leaves him playing second fiddle to Michael Johnson.
By any definition Johnson was the track and field athlete of a year which concluded here on Friday with the world governing body's annual gala dinner.

Disciplined, composed and chillingly efficient, Johnson gave in Atlanta the greatest exhibition of sprinting since Ben Johnson and Florence Griffith-Joyner rewrote the record books at the 1988 Seoul Olympics.

The Texan, who completed the first men's 200 and 400 metres Olympic double, slashed his own world record to 19.32 seconds in the Olympic final, a performance which puts him as far ahead of his contemporaries as American Griffith-Joyner in the women's event eight years ago.
In 1988 Ben Johnson set a world record in the Seoul Olympic final which was disallowed after he tested positive for an anabolic steroid.

Bailey, also born in Jamaica, gained his country's first 100 metres gold medal with a world record 9.84 seconds. But his victory, after a dramatic overture which saw defending champion Linford Christie disqualified for false starting twice, was overshadowed by Johnson's double.
Trinidad's Ato Bolden, bronze medallist in both the 100 and 200 metres, spelled out the competitors' thoughts after the 200 final.
"I said before that the winner of the 100 is the fastest man alive, " Boldon said. "But with all respect to my friend Donovan Bailey, I think now the fastest man alive is sitting next to me."
Johnson and Bailey are scheduled to meet next year over 150 metres -- a race and distance which will settle no debates, although it should certainly swell both men's bank balances.
Marie-Jose Perec, another Caribbean export, emulated Johnson in Atlanta by clinching the women's 200 and 400 metres for France.
The Guadaloupe native defeated sentimental favourite Merlene Ottey in the 200 and set an Olympic record in the 400. She was the first person to retain the Olympic 400 title.
Carl Lewis rolled back the years to take his fourth Olympic long jump title at the age of 35 against a headwind.
"This is the biggest moment of my entire career," he said. "I can't explain it or express my feelings."
Russian Svetlana Masterkova, who had taken three years out to have a baby, won the women's 800-1,500 double with surprising ease.
"I was waiting for the other girls to catch up," she said ingenuously after defeating Ana Quirot and Maria Mutola in the 800.
Maserkova went on to break world records in the 1,000 metres and mile.
Following the Games, Moroccan Salah Hissou reduced an already impresive world 10,000 metres record to 26 minutes 36.08 seconds at the Brussels grand prix.

And Daniel Komen, who could not even qualify for the Kenyan Olympic team, destroyed the world 3,000 metres record as well as recording the third fastest time over 5,000 metres and breaking the world two-mile best.
